Buried under this week’s much louder AI security story (OpenAI’s models hacking Hugging Face) was a smaller disclosure that’s arguably more useful if you’re an actual developer rather than a policy analyst: a researcher found that Claude Cowork’s Linux VM sandbox could be escaped with a single message, handing the agent full read/write access to the host Mac’s filesystem. SSH keys, cloud credentials, all of it.
I want to be precise about why this matters, because “sandbox escape” headlines tend to trigger either panic or a shrug, and neither is the right reaction. The right reaction is: this is what a sandbox escape looks like when it happens to a tool a lot of people are actually using day to day, not a theoretical benchmark scenario. Same week, same underlying failure mode: isolation boundary, single unexpected input, boundary gone, just at a completely different scale of consequence and a completely different audience.
If you build with agentic coding tools, or you’re wiring Claude, GPT, or anything else into a product where the model gets tool access, file access, or shell access, here’s the uncomfortable question this should push you to actually answer instead of assume: what’s the blast radius if the sandbox around your agent fails today?
